IMiC supplementary material

Section 8 Sensitivity analyses and additional outputs

The robustness analyses and supplementary outputs referenced from the manuscript are gathered here, grouped by analysis class. Each subsection asks a version of the same question of the primary adjusted, standardised TMLE analyses presented earlier: would the headline conclusions still hold?

  • 8.1 Unadjusted intervention effects: the same TMLE framework with covariate adjustment removed, which shows whether adjustment is doing meaningful work in the primary analyses.
  • 8.2 Unscaled (natural-unit) intervention effects: adjusted TMLE ATEs in the native assay units (e.g. g/100 mL, µg/L, µM), letting readers interpret effect magnitudes clinically. Covers all three outcome groups (primary, secondary, and tertiary/targeted metabolomics); the primary and secondary estimates correspond to manuscript Table S7.
  • 8.3 Fat-adjusted triglyceride effects (Figure S4): separating changes in triglyceride composition from transient changes in total milk fat.
  • 8.4 SuperLearner CV-AUC treatment-arm prediction (manuscript Fig. 1A): a multivariate test of whether the joint distribution of HM components carries intervention signal beyond per-component testing.
  • 8.5 PCA-based composite outcome scores (manuscript Fig. 1B): ATEs on the first principal component of each modality, asking whether each modality moved as a whole.
  • 8.6 Pathway enrichment analyses: now reported in full in §9 Reproducible pathway and enrichment analyses; only the network views and a pointer remain here.
  • 8.7 Infant growth analyses (Figure S1): intervention effects on infant anthropometry within the IMiC subsamples, as a within-trial sanity check.

Primary inference about whether intervention effects are present and consistent rests on the adjusted analyses in §5. The analyses in this chapter contextualise those findings rather than replace them.

8.1 Unadjusted intervention effects

Unadjusted estimates use the same TMLE framework but omit covariate adjustment. Where adjusted and unadjusted estimates differ, the gap may reflect confounding by baseline maternal, infant, or household characteristics, differences in sampling structure across studies and visits, or chance. Within a single randomised trial a large divergence would be surprising and would warrant a closer look at the adjustment set; these forest plots are best read alongside those in §5.

8.2 Unscaled (natural-unit) intervention effects

Unscaled estimates are adjusted TMLE ATEs reported on the native assay scale of each milk component (for example, g/100 mL for macronutrients; µg/L or mg/L for micronutrients; relative abundance for HMOs; µM for the targeted metabolomics panel). The standardised, SD-unit estimates in §5 are built for cross-component comparison. The natural-unit estimates here restate them in biologically meaningful units, so a reader can ask “how much did B3 actually go up, in mg/L?” rather than only “by how many SD units did B3 go up?”. Think of this section as the absolute-concentration view of the §5 results. The primary and secondary native-unit estimates below correspond to Table S7 of the manuscript (per-arm sample sizes, means, SDs, medians and IQRs, alongside native-unit ATEs, 95% CIs, and FDR-adjusted q-values for all primary and secondary outcomes); Table S7 does not extend to the tertiary targeted-metabolomics panel, so the tertiary native-unit ATEs at the end of this section have no manuscript table counterpart; they are reported here for completeness, sourced from the same upstream unscaled-effects run.

8.2.2 Table S7: per-arm native-unit concentrations and descriptive statistics

The full manuscript Table S7 is reproduced below as a searchable table. For every primary and secondary milk component, by study × visit × arm, it gives the sample size, the covariate-adjusted mean and 95% CI (mean, mean_cil, mean_ciu), and the raw distributional summary (raw_mean, raw_sd, raw_median, raw_q25, raw_q75) in native assay units. It provides the tabular backing for the concentration distributions in manuscript Fig. 4 and the effect estimates in Figs. 2–3.

Download: table_s7_primary_secondary_native_units.csv (long format, as shown below), or table_s7_primary_secondary_native_units_wide.csv (one row per component × study × visit, with the arms side by side).

8.3 Fat-adjusted triglyceride effects (Figure S4)

The largest tertiary-outcome signal in the manuscript is on triglycerides (TGs). In MISAME-III the same TGs were increased at 14–21 days and 3–4 months but decreased at the 1–2 month visit. This temporal inversion disappears once concentrations are expressed as a fraction of total fat content, which implies that the apparent 1–2 month decrease reflects the transient drop in total fat at that visit rather than a compositional change in the TG pool. The plot below reproduces Figure S4 (treatment-specific TG means with and without fat adjustment), and the forest plot beneath it shows the fat-adjusted ATEs behind that interpretation.

Milk-volume caveat. Total milk output was not measured in any of the three IMiC trials. The transient reduction in milk fat concentration seen at 1–2 months in MISAME-III may therefore reflect dilution from increased milk volume in the supplemented arm rather than a true reduction in fat synthesis or secretion. Concentration-based effects on macronutrients, and on any fat-dependent metabolite, should be read with this in mind: without a denominator on total daily output, a change in concentration cannot be translated cleanly into a change in infant nutrient delivery. The fat-adjusted analysis below removes one form of this confounding, proportional re-allocation across TGs, but it cannot recover the missing volume term.

Figure S4. Treatment-specific means (and 95% CIs) of milk triglycerides (N = 235 TG species from the targeted-metabolomics panel) in MISAME-III, with and without adjustment for total milk fat. Top: treatment-specific mean TG-species concentrations; points are coloured by significance of the ATE estimate, and TGs are sorted by the mean Z-scored control-arm concentration at the first visit. The reductions seen at the second timepoint in the postnatal BEP arms (panels O and U) dissipate when concentrations are expressed as a percentage of total fat (panels P and V), revealing the same TG-species pattern as at the first and third timepoints. Bottom: fat-adjusted adjusted ATEs (SD units, 95% CI) for individual TG species, confirming a consistent direction of effect across visits once total milk fat is accounted for.

8.4 SuperLearner multi-class treatment-arm prediction

The Methods describe a SuperLearner ensemble trained to predict multi-class randomised treatment-arm membership from the full set of measured primary, secondary, and tertiary HM outcomes within each study × visit. A cross-validated AUC (CV-AUC) above chance indicates that the joint distribution of HM components contains intervention signal beyond what any single component carries, and variable-importance (VIMP) measures identify which components carry most of that predictive signal.

This is the multivariate counterpart to the univariate forest plots in §5. It asks whether the per-component signals, taken together, predict arm assignment, and which components drive the prediction.

Figure 1A. Cross-validated AUC (CV-AUC) from SuperLearner ensembles trained to predict randomized treatment arm from each class of milk components (and from all classes combined), by study and milk-collection visit. CV-AUC ≈ 0.5 (dashed line) is chance-level; higher values indicate that the joint distribution of that component class carries intervention signal. B-vitamins and targeted metabolites give the strongest signals, while azithromycin-only and prenatal-BEP arms show none.

8.5 PCA-based composite outcome scores

ATEs were also estimated for the first principal component of each modality (macronutrients, B-vitamins, HMOs, bioactives, targeted metabolites). A PCA-based composite collapses correlated within-modality components into a single scalar capturing the dominant axis of variation, which makes it sensitive to coordinated multivariate shifts that may not survive per-component FDR. It offers a one-number check on whether each modality moved as a whole.

Figure 1B. Adjusted ATEs (95% CI) on the first principal component (PC1) of each milk-component class, pooled intervention vs. control, by study and visit. Effects are oriented positive for comparability across classes; filled symbols are significant after FDR correction. B-vitamin PC1 is increased across trials and timepoints, with no consistent effect on the other component classes.

8.6 Pathway enrichment analyses

The pathway- and enrichment-level interpretation of the high-dimensional milk signals now lives in its own chapter, §9 Reproducible pathway and enrichment analyses. That work covers MetaboAnalyst over-representation/MSEA of the primary, tertiary, and untargeted metabolome, Mummichog functional enrichment, and Gene Ontology enrichment of the milk proteome. It is built directly from the scripted MetaboAnalystR CSV outputs (results/metaboanalyst/, copied in by port_results.R) and covers manuscript Tables S1–S6 and the enrichment panels of Fig. 3B, Fig. 5B, and Fig. 6A–C. It replaces an earlier placeholder here that loaded not-yet-produced pathway_enrichment_*.RDS objects.

The compositional fatty-acid enrichment of intervention-responsive triglycerides (manuscript Table S3 / Fig. 5C) is the compositional companion to the fat-adjusted triglyceride analysis in §8.3 above; its reproducible table is in §9.5.

8.7 Infant growth analyses (Figure S1)

Here we report the effects of maternal nutritional supplementation on infant anthropometric outcomes within the IMiC subsamples of each trial: length-for-age z-score (LAZ), weight-for-length z-score (WLZ), weight-for-age z-score (WAZ), head-circumference-for-age z-score (HCAZ), and mid-upper-arm-circumference-for-age z-score (MUACZ). Estimates use the same covariate-adjusted TMLE framework as the primary milk-component analyses. These growth analyses act as within-trial sanity checks. They document whether the IMiC subsample is a plausible, representative window onto the parent trial, and they set the manuscript’s HM-composition findings against the corresponding infant phenotype.

Negative-control note (ELICIT). Infant azithromycin and infant nicotinamide were administered only after 6 months of age. Their effects on the 1-month and 5-month HM-collection visits are therefore null by design and act as a within-trial negative control on the analytic pipeline. Any non-null estimate in those contrasts should be read as noise.

Figure S1. Adjusted intervention effects (ATE on anthropometric z-score, with 95% CI) on infant length-for-age (LAZ), weight-for-length (WLZ), weight-for-age (WAZ), head-circumference-for-age (HCAZ), and MUAC-for-age (MUACZ), by study, randomized contrast, and infant age at measurement. Filled symbols are significant after FDR correction. In ELICIT, infant azithromycin and nicotinamide were administered after 6 months, so their effects at the 1- and 5-month visits are null by design and serve as a within-trial negative control.
